title: Messy Sources, Clean Datasets
objective: After this lesson you will be able to classify any PDF as text-native, scanned, or hybrid; predict which extraction path each class needs; and state the loader pipeline (route → extract → validate → clean → chunk → evaluate) that the next four lessons fill in.
why: Every data project spends ~80% of its effort on loading and cleaning, yet tutorials start from pristine CSVs. Real sources are PDFs with missing text layers, custom font encodings, two-column layouts, and scanned pages stapled between digital ones. Classifying before extracting is the single decision that prevents weeks of rework: wrong path first means rebuilding everything later.

blocks.text: PDFs are pictures with optional text taped on

A PDF page is a **canvas of positioned glyphs and vector shapes** — not a document with paragraphs. The readable text you select is an optional **text layer** (characters + coordinates) sitting over the visuals. Extraction reads that layer, never the picture. No layer (scans, photos, flattened exports) means nothing to extract — pixels must become text first via OCR. Screen appearance proves rendering, never extractability.

rows: Select text; extract a page and read raw strings — coherent sentences
Per-page routing: text path where layers exist, OCR elsewhere
Extracts as mojibake despite selectable text

blocks.text: The triage routine (ten minutes that save weeks)

For any new PDF folder: (1) sample pages across the document (covers lie — middles differ); (2) test selectability and extract raw strings; (3) check fonts (embedded? custom encodings?); (4) detect layout (single vs multi-column, tables present?); (5) record the class **per page range**, because hybrids dominate real corpora. The output is a triage table, not a feeling — and every downstream choice references it.

blocks.caption: Routing is a function of evidence — encode the triage table, don't eyeball it

blocks.text: The router above is deliberately crude — real triage adds layout and table detection — but its shape is the course's thesis: **decisions from evidence, recorded per page range**. The dossier becomes the project's first artifact, and every later stage (extraction settings, validation strictness, chunk metadata) keys off the class recorded here.

Five stages, one direction: **route** (this lesson: classify + record) → **extract** (Ch.2: text with order intact) → **validate** (Ch.3: schema + quarantine) → **clean** (Ch.4: normalize, repair, standardize, dedupe) → **chunk + evaluate** (Ch.5: overlap chunks with page metadata, TF-IDF retrieval check). Each stage's output is the next stage's input — and rejects at any stage carry reasons forward, never vanish.

blocks.caption: The OpenDataLoader pipeline
nodes: Route: classify per page range, record dossier
Extract: text with reading order + page numbers
Validate: schema check, quarantine rejects with reasons
Chunk + evaluate: overlap chunks, TF-IDF hit-rate

items: PDFs render pixels; extraction reads the optional text layer — looks prove nothing
Classify per page range (text/scanned/hybrid/broken), record a dossier, route from evidence
Pipeline: route → extract → validate → clean → chunk + evaluate; rejects carry reasons forward

exercise.prompt: You receive a 20-page product manual: pages 1–3 extract cleanly with embedded fonts; 4–9 return empty strings; page 10 extracts 31 garbled characters; 11–20 extract fluently but list no embedded fonts. (a) Run the router on all four ranges in the playground. (b) Write the triage dossier (class + path per range, one evidence line each). (c) State the one range you would investigate first by hand, and what you would check.
hints: Router inputs per range: {textChars, embeddedFonts}. 1–3: thousands + true. 4–9: zero. 10: 31 + true. 11–20: thousands + false.
Classes: text-native (1–3), scanned (4–9), suspicious (10), broken-encoding-likely (11–20 → OCR fallback or mapping repair).
Investigate page 10 first by hand: 31 garbled characters with fonts present smells like a scanned figure page or encoding edge — zoom in and decide OCR vs repair before batch settings touch it.
exercise.why: Triage is evidence-first project management: the dossier turns a scary folder into four routed work items with per-range settings. Page 10 teaches the meta-lesson — anomalies get human eyes before batch automation, because one weird page reveals the corpus's failure modes.

quiz.q: A PDF looks perfect but extraction returns empty strings. Diagnosis?
options: Scanned/image-only: pixels without a text layer — route to OCR
quiz.explain: Rendering proves pixels; extraction needs the text layer. Test selectability and raw extracted strings — looks never count as evidence.

quiz.q: Why classify per page range instead of per document?
options: Real corpora are hybrid: covers, scans, and digital pages mix — one global setting mistreats most pages
quiz.explain: Hybrids dominate: a single pipeline setting fits no range well. Per-range routing lets text pages skip OCR costs while scans get the preprocessing they need.

quiz.q: Fluent extraction volume but no embedded fonts. Meaning?
options: Broken-encoding risk: glyphs render via system substitution while extracted codes mislead — OCR fallback or mapping repair
quiz.explain: Volume without font evidence is the mojibake warning light. Verify by reading raw strings, then route to repair-or-OCR before trusting a single character.

summary: Classify first (text/scanned/hybrid/broken per page range), record the dossier, route from evidence. The pipeline — route, extract, validate, clean, chunk+evaluate — turns the 80% grind into five manageable stages.
